result: Abrams et al. (2021) reported that dietary supplementation with L-leucine, insulin, and sucrose induces appendage regeneration in jellyfish, flies, and mice—species previously thought to lack regenerative capacity. This finding was interpreted as evidence for a conserved, unlockable regenerative ability across non-regenerating animals.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C5, and C6 accurately summarize the findings and conclusions of Abrams et al. (2021) as cited. These are factual statements about what was reported in the prior work, supported by appropriate citations.

result: Insect regeneration capacity varies by metamorphosis type: hemimetabolous insects (incomplete metamorphosis) can regenerate limbs during molting, while holometabolous insects (complete metamorphosis) can regenerate imaginal discs during development but not adult appendages after final metamorphosis, likely due to epigenetic silencing of developmental programs.
evaluation: Claims C7-C19 provide well-established background on insect regeneration biology, supported by appropriate citations (Yang et al. 2016; Bando et al. 2018; Fox et al. 2020; Harris et al. 2020; Repiso et al. 2011). This represents accepted scientific knowledge in the field.

result: The authors replicated the Abrams et al. experimental protocol using Canton-S Drosophila, amputating 1,283 hind legs at the tibia midpoint, with 240 flies on control food and 843 on treated food (5 mM L-leucine, 5 mM L-glutamine, 0.1 mg/ml insulin), examining outcomes after three weeks using blinded bright-field microscopy.
evaluation: Claims C20-C22, C28-C31, C103-C107 describe the experimental design with appropriate detail. The methods appear rigorous, including blinding (C31), appropriate sample sizes given the reported 1% effect (C21-C22), and precise inclusion criteria (C104). The experimental design is well-documented.

result: No cuticle regeneration was observed in either control or treated groups after three weeks. All tibia stumps showed bristle deterioration and darkened cuticle indicating necrosis. A white blob appeared at the cut site in 4% of control and 3% of treated cases, similar to the frequency reported by Abrams et al.
evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C24, C32-C37 report clear negative results with appropriate quantification (Table 1, Figure 1). The similar outcomes between control and treated groups (C33) and comparable white blob frequency to Abrams et al. (C35-C36) strengthen the findings. The blinded assessment (C31) reduces bias.

result: Bristle sensory neurons, labeled with ChAT-Gal4>UAS-GFP, were present immediately after amputation but absent three weeks later in both control and treated groups (n=200 legs). Neurons in proximal leg segments appeared normal, indicating cell death was confined to the amputated segment.
evaluation: Claims C38-C45 describe well-controlled experiments using genetic reporters to track specific cell types. The use of fluorescent labeling (C40) provides direct visualization of neurons. Results show no difference between control and treated groups (C43) and appropriate internal controls (C44). Figure 2A supports these findings.

result: Phalloidin staining revealed no muscle tissue in tibia stumps three weeks after amputation in either control or treated groups, while muscle staining in proximal leg segments remained normal.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 use appropriate methodology (phalloidin for F-actin/muscle) with clear negative results documented in Figure 2B and Table 1. The presence of normal muscle staining proximally (C48) serves as an important positive control, demonstrating the staining worked and cell death was localized.

result: DAPI staining showed no nuclei in tibia stumps three weeks post-amputation (n=137 control, n=544 treated), while proximal segments had normal staining. This pattern of localized cell death is consistent with prior work in cockroaches, suggesting the amputated stump is an empty cuticle tube devoid of living cells.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 provide strong evidence for complete cell death using nuclear staining with large sample sizes. The consistency with prior work (C52, Bodenstein 1955) and normal proximal staining (C51) strengthen the conclusion. Figure 2C supports these findings. The inference that the stump is empty (C54) is reasonable given the absence of any cellular markers.

result: The white blob at amputation sites occurred at similar frequency (3-4%) in both control and treated groups. EdU labeling showed no incorporation in tibia stumps or white blobs, while positive control gut tissue showed robust EdU staining, indicating the white blob is not a proliferating regeneration blastema.
evaluation: Claims C55-C64 use EdU incorporation as an established marker for cell proliferation (C60-C61) with appropriate positive controls (C62, gut tissue). The absence of EdU in stumps and white blobs (C63) combined with occurrence in both control and treated groups (C58) strongly argues against regeneration. The methodology is sound and well-controlled.

result: The white blob consists of bacteria, not regenerated tissue. DAPI-stained nuclei in the blob were ~1/10th the size of fly cells (hemocytes, neurons, muscle, imaginal disc cells) and yeast, but matched the size of bacteria from fly excrement. The blob did not stain with phalloidin, consistent with bacterial cytoskeleton (MreB) that doesn't bind phalloidin.
evaluation: Claims C4, C26, C65-C76 provide multiple lines of converging evidence: nuclear size comparisons across multiple cell types (C66, C69, C71-C72, Figure 3E-J), absence of phalloidin staining (C73) consistent with bacterial cytoskeleton biology (C74), and lack of EdU incorporation explained by bacteria feeding on dead tissue (C75). The size comparison methodology is rigorous and the conclusion is well-supported, though the speculation about EdU (C75) is acknowledged as such.

result: Fly legs do not regenerate after amputation. Three weeks post-amputation, tibias were completely devoid of neurons, muscles, and nuclei in both control and treated groups, appearing as hollow cuticle tubes. These findings are consistent with established literature that adult holometabolous insects do not regenerate lost ectodermal structures.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 synthesize the experimental findings (neurons, muscle, DAPI, EdU all negative) into a clear conclusion supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. The consistency with prior literature (C82, Fox et al. 2020; Repiso et al. 2011) and lack of difference between control and treated groups (C81) strongly support this conclusion.

result: The authors speculate that Abrams et al.'s conclusions were based on inaccurate measurement techniques, as detecting a 1% phenotype requires exceptional precision. Potential issues include imprecise quantification of sub-mm cuticle changes, unclear blinding procedures, and possible methodological differences (razor vs. scissors, Canton-S sub-strains), though Abrams et al. reported effects across genetic backgrounds.
evaluation: Claims C83-C90 offer reasonable speculation about sources of discrepancy but lack direct evidence. The critique of measurement precision (C84-C85) and blinding (C86) is valid, but the authors acknowledge their own potential limitations (sample size for rare events). The methodological differences (C87-C88) are minor and unlikely to explain the complete absence of regeneration. This represents informed speculation rather than demonstrated fact.

result: The authors question the biological plausibility of the Abrams et al. findings, noting that cuticle regrowth without living cells is implausible, and that ingested insulin would be degraded in the gut (though direct contact between stump and food remains possible).
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 raise valid mechanistic concerns. The absence of living cells (C91) is well-documented in this study and makes regeneration implausible. The insulin degradation point (C92) is supported by citation (Winter 1923) and represents basic biochemistry, though the alternative mechanism (C93) is appropriately presented as speculation.

result: The authors' results cast doubt on Abrams et al.'s conclusion that dietary supplements induce Drosophila leg regeneration and undermine the broader claim of a conserved regenerative strategy across non-regenerating animals. The authors did not attempt to replicate jellyfish or mouse experiments due to lack of expertise.
evaluation: Claims C94-C97 represent reasonable conclusions from the experimental data. The Drosophila results clearly contradict Abrams et al. (C94, C96), and the authors appropriately limit their conclusions to the system they studied (C95). The inference that flaws in Drosophila experiments undermine the broader conclusion (C96) is logical but limited by not testing other species.

result: The authors argue their work has broader implications because model organism results often motivate human studies, FDA-approved ingredients could enable unregulated supplement sales, and Abrams et al. have filed a patent. They call for additional scrutiny and independent replication of the dietary supplement regeneration claims.
evaluation: Claims C98-C101 appropriately contextualize the importance of rigorous replication. The translational pathway concern (C98) is valid, the regulatory concern (C99) is reasonable given FDA approval of individual ingredients, and the patent filing (C100) is factual. The call for additional scrutiny (C101) is appropriate given the contradictory findings.

result: Fly gut exhibits homeostatic cell proliferation during the adult stage, serving as a positive control for EdU incorporation experiments.
evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by citation (Xiang et al. 2017) and experimental validation (C62, Figure 3B showing robust EdU staining). This demonstrates the EdU labeling protocol was working properly.
